strengths: First scalable hierarchical framework jointly generating hypergraph topology and features, addressing a genuine gap left by prior work (HYGENE)
Novel node budget mechanism provides principled control over local growth consistency across scales, elegantly handling uneven expansion rates
Intelligent adaptation of minibatch OT-coupling to hierarchical setting with rigorous justification (Propositions 10, 12) while maintaining computational efficiency
Significant practical scalability advantage: only method handling point clouds with 1024 nodes while competing methods (DiGress, DeFoG) fail with OOM
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse domains (synthetic hypergraphs, 3D meshes, point clouds) with thorough ablation studies demonstrating necessity of both components
Excellent reproducibility support through detailed algorithms (1-5), implementation details, hyperparameter specifications, and complexity analysis
weaknesses: Improvements over HYGENE baseline are often modest on key metrics (e.g., Tree hypergraph node numbers both 0.000; Ego degree distribution gains ~2% valid increase with marginal metric improvements)

Method still struggles with very large structures per Section 4.4; high variance in some results (point cloud Ratio: 67.311±44.903) and noisy performance on ModelNet (Node Num: 0.846±1.009) suggest instability

Feature modeling fundamentally limited to simple distributions (3D coordinates); no demonstration with categorical, multi-modal, or heterogeneous features, limiting applicability to stated molecular design motivation

Several unjustified design choices lacking ablation: weighted-average for cluster features, budget splitting tie-breaking rule (Remark 7), graph inpainting constraints, zero matrix initialization; alternatives unexplored

Weak baseline for featured mesh generation: only one sequential alternative tested; no strong joint flat baseline attempted; graph inpainting constraints add strong assumptions without sensitivity analysis
Theoretical contributions incremental: Proposition 3 is standard MSE minimization calculus; Propositions 10, 12 straightforward applications of existing OT theory; main novelty is engineering
Presentation of core ideas delayed by heavy formalism; dense notation (multiple tildes, overloaded B) in Section 3 obscures intuition; conditional independence assumption (Eq. 6) lacks justification

strengths: Addresses a real problem: existing hierarchical methods ignore features while flat methods don't scale
Technically sound with formal definitions, proofs, and rigorous experimental setup including ablations and complexity analysis
Comprehensive evaluation across diverse datasets (synthetic hypergraphs, 3D meshes, point clouds) with extensive supplementary material
Node budget mechanism provides intuitive local growth control and shows consistent improvements in ablations
Demonstrates clear improvements over sequential baselines on 3D mesh generation (~50% better Chamfer distance)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily extends HYGENE [10] with features; core contributions (budgets, minibatch OT-coupling) are incremental engineering rather than conceptual advances
Scalability claims are overstated—acknowledged to 'struggle with very large hypergraphs' and training is 'computationally expensive,' contradicting the main motivation
Marginal improvements over strongest baseline (HYGENE): spectral metrics often within noise margins; point cloud comparisons unfairly advantage hierarchical methods via OOM of flat baselines

Feature generation severely limited to continuous coordinates; no support for categorical/multi-modal attributes despite motivating applications; Proposition 3 lacks justification for why MSE-minimizing averaging is good for generation

Weak experimental baselines on synthetic hypergraphs (image-based diffusion, VAE, GAN); only HYGENE is relevant; minibatch OT-coupling shows inconsistent benefits across datasets with ablations suggesting node budget dominates
Joint vs sequential generation motivation underdeveloped—only validated on Manifold40 meshes; missing analysis of why joint learning helps and whether this generalizes to other feature types

Evaluation metrics inconsistent across tasks (structural metrics vs Chamfer distance vs graph metrics) making cross-dataset quality assessment difficult; no statistical significance testing despite reported improvements often within 2σ

Missing analysis on sensitivity to hyperparameters (reduction fraction, λ varying 0.1-0.3 per dataset suggests potential overfitting), out-of-distribution generation capability, and ablation on coarsening strategy choice

strengths: Novel node budget mechanism that provides intuitive local growth constraints and is theoretically justified (Proposition 3)
Clever adaptation of minibatch OT-coupling to hierarchical graph generation with proper theoretical justification (Propositions 10, 12)
Addresses genuine gap in literature: first scalable hierarchical framework for joint topology and feature generation in hypergraphs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple diverse domains (synthetic hypergraphs, 3D meshes, point clouds) with clear improvements over HYGENE
Only method capable of handling point cloud datasets at scale (baselines OOM), demonstrating practical scalability advantage
Rigorous mathematical framework with formal definitions, sound proofs, and detailed algorithmic descriptions (Algorithms 1-5)
Honest and clear discussion of limitations; extensive supplementary material supports reproducibility
Strong empirical results on featured 3D meshes showing joint generation (Chamfer 0.073/0.049) significantly outperforms sequential baseline (0.143/0.117)
weaknesses: Scalability claims vs. reality mismatch: paper motivates by large-scale generation but Section 4.4 acknowledges struggles with very large hypergraphs and graphs; point cloud results show high variance and poor metric values (Ratio 67-84), suggesting method may scale computationally but not in solution quality

Severely limited feature modalities: only 3D coordinates evaluated; framework explicitly stated to assume 'simple feature distributions' with categorical/multi-modal features requiring 'additional modeling components'; undermines motivation for molecular design applications requiring atom/bond types

Computational cost under-analyzed despite scalability focus: paper mentions training is 'computationally expensive' but provides no runtime comparisons, wall-clock timings, or practical cost analysis relative to baselines

Weak baseline comparisons for featured data: 3D meshes only compared to author-designed sequential baseline (potential strawman); PolyGen and MeshGPT mentioned but not compared; point cloud baselines fail with OOM providing no quality comparison

Limited analysis of method behavior: unclear why OT-coupling helps SBM/ManifoldNet but not Ego/Tree; no intuition for when budget mechanism matters most; point cloud quality metrics concerning (Ratio metric 67-84 indicates poor reconstruction)

Experimental design concerns: no convergence analysis for 1M training steps; hyperparameter selection process unjustified (λ varies across experiments); Algorithm 5 contains ad-hoc heuristics (lines 13-14) with unknown sensitivity; max cluster sizes of 2-3 presented as constraint without analyzing impact

Theoretical contributions relatively straightforward: Proposition 3 is basic calculus; Propositions 8, 10, 12 are useful but not deep; no formal analysis of when hierarchical approach preserves graph properties or characterization of failure modes

Incomplete evaluation: no diversity/mode coverage metrics for generated samples; no generation time comparisons; large variance on some datasets (e.g., ModelNet Piano 0.846±1.009) suggests instability on difficult instances; modest dataset sizes

strengths: First hierarchical method to jointly generate topology and features for graphs and hypergraphs, addressing a real limitation of prior work
Demonstrates significant practical scalability advantage: handles point clouds with ~1400 nodes where state-of-the-art methods (DiGress, DeFoG) fail with OOM

Well-motivated and theoretically grounded technical contributions: hierarchical scale encoding with recursive splitting (Prop. 1), multi-scale OT coupling (Props. 2-3) with formal optimality results, graph inpainting justified by gradient dilution analysis (Prop. 4)
Comprehensive experimental validation: 9 diverse datasets with appropriate metrics, thorough ablations demonstrating component importance, error bars over 5 runs, honest limitations discussion
Quasi-linear O((n+m+k)log n) complexity achieved versus quadratic complexity of flat methods
Clear presentation with well-organized exposition, informative visualizations, and complete algorithmic details in appendices
weaknesses: Inconsistent experimental results undermine claims: FAHNES achieves only 50.0%±5.0 valid on SBM graphs versus 90.0%±5.1 for DeFoG; 96.7%±6.2 on planar graphs versus 99.5%±1.0 for DeFoG. Method trades small-scale quality for large-scale scalability, limiting practical applicability

High variance and instability in results: ModelNet Bookshelf Node Num shows 0.135±0.276 (coefficient of variation ~200%), Bench point clouds ratio 73.3±22.2, raising concerns about training stability and generalization

Despite 'feature-aware' title, restricted to continuous features only (3D coordinates). Categorical/multi-modal features require 'additional modeling components' per authors. This significantly limits real-world applicability to graphs with diverse attribute types

Fundamental scalability limitation unresolved: method 'still struggles' with 'very large hypergraphs' like ModelNet (50-180 nodes) per Section 5.4, contradicting quasi-linear complexity claims for practical scenarios

Incomplete theoretical justification: conditional independence assumption (Eq. 9) lacks detailed rationale; choice to sum node scales as cluster encoding presented as intuitive but no deeper justification; alternative aggregations unexplored

Incremental contribution: core coarse-to-fine framework from prior work (Bergmeister et al. 2024, Gailhard et al. 2025); main novelty is adding feature generation via standard averaging and flow matching

No statistical significance testing provided despite large error bars; no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters (only one reduction fraction range [0.1,0.3] tested); multi-scale OT coupling approximation (restricting to same-cluster permutations) impact not analyzed
Multi-scale OT coupling practical compromise poorly analyzed: restricting permutations to same-cluster nodes may lose optimal alignments, but frequency and impact of this limitation not quantified

strengths: First hierarchical method to jointly generate topology and features for graphs and hypergraphs, addressing a real gap in prior work
Theoretically grounded with formal propositions justifying design choices (optimal feature merging, OT properties, gradient masking)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dataset types (synthetic, real-world, 3D meshes, point clouds) with extensive ablations
Achieves O((n+m+k)log n) complexity, better than quadratic flat methods
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging scalability and feature type restrictions
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: hierarchical coarsening-expansion is from prior work; main contributions (scale encoding, feature addition) are incremental extensions rather than fundamental innovations

Mixed experimental results: marginal improvements over baselines on featured hypergraphs (Table 4 shows only modest gains over weak sequential baseline); loses to DeFoG on unfeatured small graphs (Table 2); point cloud results show 22.2% coverage with no baseline comparison

Scalability claims significantly overstated: largest tested graph is ~1400 nodes; ModelNet Piano shows 0.846±1.009 error (extremely high variance); explicit admission in Section 5.4 that 'scalability remains challenging when both number of nodes and structural complexity grow substantially' directly contradicts marketing

Ablation studies (Table 5) reveal design concerns: scale encoding and OT coupling hurt performance on tree structures and show highly task-dependent benefits, suggesting components aren't as well-motivated as claimed

Multi-scale OT coupling unjustified: adds 4% overhead for only 2-6 local permutations per cluster; ablation shows inconsistent benefits (ManifoldNet Bench: ChamDist gets worse when coupling removed); restriction to local clusters defeats purpose

Insufficient feature quality analysis: Chamfer distance only measures spatial coverage not feature fidelity; no feature distribution comparisons; joint generation only modestly improves over sequential baseline, undercutting the paper's main claim

Missing critical experiments: no molecular graph generation despite motivation; no very-large-scale tests (5K+ nodes); no comparison with domain-specific mesh methods; no feature type beyond continuous 3D coordinates

Hyperparameter sensitivity unexplored: λ varies by task (0.1, 0.3) without justification; different hyperparameters per dataset (Appendix E) suggest lack of robustness; no sensitivity analysis provided
Design choices inadequately justified: why restrict merges to ≤2 nodes? why separate expansion from refinement? why does scale encoding hurt on trees? lack of intuition beyond empirical numbers
Limited applicability: cannot handle categorical or heterogeneous features (acknowledged in Section 5.4); no experiments on natural featured graph domains like molecules

strengths: First hierarchical framework to jointly generate topology and features for both graphs and hypergraphs, addressing a genuine gap in prior work
Theoretically grounded with formal definitions (Defs 1-5), rigorous proofs (Props 1-4), and complexity analysis proving O((n+m+k)log n) quasi-linear complexity

Novel hierarchical scale encoding elegantly solves uneven growth problem and multi-scale OT coupling is principled adaptation of minibatch OT with theoretical guarantees on marginal preservation and variance reduction

Comprehensive experiments across 14 diverse datasets with multiple metrics, ablation studies, extensive appendices, and reproducible implementation details; only method that scales to large point clouds without OOM
Broad applicability demonstrated across synthetic hypergraphs, 3D meshes, point clouds, and molecular/protein graphs with unified framework
Well-organized presentation with clear motivation, intuitive figures (especially Fig. 2 and 3), formal mathematical framework, and honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: coarsening-expansion framework reuses Bergmeister et al. (2024)/Gailhard et al. (2025), flow matching from Lipman et al. (2023), and scale encoding is relatively straightforward; incremental rather than foundational contribution

Mixed experimental results: FAHNES underperforms or matches baselines on small-to-medium graphs (SBM 50% valid vs DeFoG 90%, planar 96.7% vs 99.5%), with significant advantages only on large-scale point clouds (~1400 nodes); improvements on 3D meshes are modest

Scalability claims only partially validated: paper acknowledges struggles with 'very large' graphs/hypergraphs; largest tested datasets (~1400 nodes) not extraordinarily large by modern standards; quasi-linear complexity not revolutionary for graphs

Experimental design limitations: weak baselines for featured generation (Sequential, WGAN, VAE), limited ablation studies (only scale encoding and OT on 4 datasets; missing ablations on spectral conditioning, perturbed expansion, coarsening strategy), and some metrics may favor hierarchical methods by design

Technical justification gaps: conditional independence assumption in Eq. 9 lacks rigorous justification; scale encoding design choices (why summation vs alternatives) not explored; multi-scale OT coupling overhead analysis incomplete; Algorithm 5 thresholds (1.66, 2.33) appear ad-hoc

Feature handling limited to continuous distributions with no guidance for categorical/heterogeneous/multi-modal features; assumes 3D coordinates rather than rich semantic attributes, limiting applicability to many real-world graphs

Presentation density: core novel contributions buried in incremental improvements; many orthogonal techniques (spectral conditioning, graph inpainting, perturbed expansion) dilute focus on primary contributions; main message could be clearer
